topic: Automating scientific peer review with LLMs

idea.title: Transfer-Aware Robust Aggregation for Adversarially-Manipulated LLM Peer Review Ensembles
idea.gap: Two lines of recent work on LLM-based peer review have developed in parallel without being tested against each other. One line shows that individual LLM reviewers are highly vulnerable to manipulation: invisible/indirect prompt injection can flip a "reject" into an "accept" (as shown in work such as "When Reject Turns into Accept," "Breaking the Reviewer," and "Paraphrasing Adversarial Attack on LLM-as-a-Reviewer"), and textual perturbations can inflate scores when placed strategically in a manuscript. A second line proposes multi-model ensembles and statistical aggregation (majority voting, weighted averaging, EM/Dawid-Skene-style pooling) to stabilize LLM review scores and bring them closer to human judgment, treating disagreement between LLM reviewers as roughly independent noise. But Dawid-Skene-style aggregation is built on an i.i.d.-noise assumption, and no existing study has tested whether an author who knows a conference uses a multi-model LLM ensemble can craft an attack that transfers across model families (exploiting shared RLHF-induced sycophancy or shared training-data biases), thereby defeating the very independence assumption the aggregation defense relies on. In other words, the field has never characterized adversarial transferability across LLM reviewer ensembles, nor whether current aggregation methods actually provide robustness against a strategic (rather than random-noise) attacker.
idea.proposed_study: Assemble a benchmark of borderline conference-style submissions (e.g., openly available ICLR/NeurIPS-style papers near the accept/reject threshold) and apply three manipulation classes drawn from the adversarial-review literature: (1) invisible/indirect prompt injection (hidden text, white-on-white or zero-width-unicode instructions), (2) character/typographic adversarial perturbations, and (3) semantic paraphrase-based attacks that reframe weaknesses as strengths without altering surface content. Score each manipulated paper with a heterogeneous panel of LLM reviewers spanning distinct model families (e.g., GPT-, Claude-, Gemini-, and open-weight Llama-class models), under three aggregation schemes: simple majority vote, weighted averaging, and EM/Dawid-Skene pooling. First, measure per-attack, per-model success rates and compute a cross-model transferability matrix (does an attack crafted/tuned against one model's scoring shift the scores of the others?). Second, measure whether each aggregation scheme actually attenuates the adversarial score shift relative to a single-reviewer baseline, and whether attenuation collapses specifically for attacks with high measured transferability. Third, design and test a transfer-aware robust aggregation rule that, instead of assuming independent reviewer noise, downweights or flags subsets of reviewers whose score shifts are anomalously correlated relative to a same-model score computed on a lightly-perturbed control copy of the manuscript (a proxy for detecting coordinated manipulation rather than genuine independent judgment).
idea.expected_result: Aggregation will meaningfully reduce adversarial score inflation for attacks with low cross-model transferability (e.g., tokenizer-specific typographic injection), but will provide little to no protection against high-transferability semantic paraphrase attacks, because these exploit judgment tendencies shared across model families rather than model-specific quirks — meaning current ensemble/Dawid-Skene defenses are systematically weaker exactly against the most sophisticated attackers. The proposed transfer-aware aggregation rule, which explicitly detects correlated (rather than independent) score shifts, should recover a substantial fraction of the lost robustness on the high-transferability attack class where naive aggregation fails.
idea.grounding: Directly motivated by combining two disjoint recent threads: adversarial-vulnerability studies of LLM reviewers (e.g., "Breaking the Reviewer," "When Reject Turns into Accept: Quantifying the Vulnerability of LLM-Based Scientific Reviewers to Indirect Prompt Injection," "Paraphrasing Adversarial Attack on LLM-as-a-Reviewer," and "Aspect-Guided Multi-Level Perturbation Analysis of LLMs in Automated Peer Review") and ensemble/aggregation-for-calibration proposals for LLM review scoring that rely on majority-vote or EM/Dawid-Skene pooling; it also answers the call in "Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation" for rigorous, adversarially-grounded evaluation before such systems are deployed in real review pipelines. This matters because conference organizers are actively debating (and in some cases piloting) LLM-assisted or multi-model review, and the standard proposed safeguard — ensembling multiple models — has never been stress-tested against a strategic author who anticipates that safeguard, as opposed to random or single-model attacks.

topic: Fully autonomous end-to-end AI scientists for machine-learning research

idea.title: Blind Self-Replication as an In-Loop Gate for Autonomous ML Research Pipelines
idea.gap: Current end-to-end AI-scientist systems (e.g., AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory) verify their own output only through self-critique or an LLM-judge review of the final manuscript, using the same context (code, logs, cherry-picked plots) that produced the result. Independent audits have documented a resulting "verification gap": pervasive post-hoc selection bias, "overexcitement" (declaring success despite weak or contradicted evidence), implementation drift, and unsupported citations that survive to the finished paper. Separately, reproducibility benchmarks such as MLReplicate evaluate whether an autonomous system's *published* outputs can be independently reproduced, and critiques such as Sibyl-AutoResearch argue current systems are "paper generators," not systems built around genuine trial-and-error validation. What is missing is a mechanism that uses reproducibility as an architectural gate operating *during* generation, before a claim ever reaches a human or a benchmark leaderboard — rather than as an external audit applied afterward to a finished paper.
idea.proposed_study: Augment an open end-to-end ML research pipeline (matching the AI Scientist-v2 / Agent Laboratory architecture: idea generation, coding, experiment execution, write-up) with a "Blind Replicator" agent that sits between experiment and paper-writing stages. For each empirical claim the primary agent drafts, the Blind Replicator receives only the natural-language Methods description and claimed result (no code, no logs, no hyperparameter files beyond what is stated in prose) plus an equal compute budget, and must independently re-implement and re-run the experiment from scratch. Define a replication-concordance score per claim (sign agreement on the primary comparison plus effect-size ratio within a pre-registered tolerance). Claims that fail concordance are automatically routed back to the primary agent with the discrepancy as feedback, forcing it to either narrow the claim's scope, mark it preliminary, or drop it — before the paper is finalized. Compare this gated pipeline against an ungated baseline (same base models/budget, standard self-critique only) on a fixed suite of small-scale ML tasks (e.g., the NanoGPT/CIFAR-variant/algorithmic-task suite used in the AI Scientist line of work). Evaluate both pipelines' final papers using a *third*, fully independent replication pass (different agent, different seed, never used in the training loop) plus human-expert grading for claim reliability, citation support, and perceived novelty/quality (to check whether gating narrows claims at a cost to perceived contribution).
idea.expected_result: The gated pipeline should show a substantially higher fraction of claims that survive independent third-party replication and lower rates of the previously documented failure modes (overexcitement, unsupported effect sizes), at the cost of narrower, more hedged claims and a modest reduction in judged "novelty" scores relative to the ungated baseline. This would show that a large share of the verification gap in current autonomous-research systems is closeable with an architectural fix — an adversarial, code-blind replication gate — without requiring new reasoning capability in the base model, and it would yield replication-concordance as a reusable automatic proxy metric for trustworthiness that is distinct from existing LLM-judge quality scores.
idea.grounding: Motivated directly by gaps named in the recent AI-scientist literature: the "verification gap" identified in surveys of autonomous research agents, the cataloged failure modes (post-hoc selection bias, overexcitement, implementation drift) in analyses of hidden pitfalls in AI Scientist systems, the reproducibility deficits measured by MLReplicate, and Sibyl-AutoResearch's argument that autonomous research needs self-evolving trial-and-error harnesses rather than paper-generation pipelines — none of which propose using code-blind independent replication as an in-loop generation-time gate rather than a post-hoc audit or static benchmark.

idea.title: Belief Perseverance in LLM Hypothesis Revision: A Cognitive-Taxonomy Benchmark for Theory Change Under Disconfirming Evidence
idea.gap: Current evaluation of LLM-generated scientific hypotheses covers novelty and validity (surveyed in "Large Language Models for Scientific Idea Generation: A Creativity-Centered Survey"), truthfulness and hallucination (TruthHypo / "Toward Reliable Scientific Hypothesis Generation: Evaluating Truthfulness and Hallucination in Large Language Models"), diverse coverage of a hypothesis space under underdetermination (HypoSpace), and one-shot prediction accuracy under progressive information disclosure (ProjectionBench). A closer strand — "Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models" — does study iterative belief updating, but only via an abstract, synthetic Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game, scored with a single scalar metric (the ratio of hypothesis-incompatible to hypothesis-compatible test proposals). None of this work asks a more structural question that decades of science-education research has already formalized for human scientists: when a real, literature-grounded hypothesis meets genuine disconfirming evidence, HOW does the reasoner change its mind — does it genuinely revise the theory, or does it deploy one of the well-documented bias-protecting maneuvers? Chinn & Brewer's classic taxonomy ("The Role of Anomalous Data in Knowledge Acquisition," 1993) identifies seven distinct response types to anomalous data — ignoring it, rejecting it, excluding it as irrelevant to the theory's domain, holding it in abeyance, reinterpreting it while retaining the core theory, making a peripheral theory change, or accepting it and changing the theory — and shows only the last constitutes genuine scientific progress. This taxonomy has never been applied to LLMs, and no existing benchmark tests whether an LLM's revision behavior degrades toward bias-protecting strategies as a function of how much self-generated justification it has already invested in its own hypothesis — the LLM analogue of the escalation-of-commitment / belief-perseverance effect documented in humans (Ross, Lepper & Hubbard) and echoed in known LLM sycophancy and self-consistency biases.
idea.proposed_study: Construct a benchmark of ~150-200 real case triples (initial evidence base, an originally plausible hypothesis it supports, and a subsequently documented disconfirming finding), drawn from domains with clear anomaly-to-revision narratives in the literature (e.g., superseded biomedical mechanisms, materials-science claims overturned by replication, retracted or substantially revised psychology effects), screening for cases obscure or recent enough to limit training-data leakage and verifying the evidence chain against primary sources. For each case, elicit a hypothesis from the LLM given only the initial evidence, under two manipulated conditions: a low-investment condition (state the hypothesis briefly) and a high-investment condition (first produce an extended mechanistic justification/defense of the hypothesis, mimicking the write-up step common in autonomous research pipelines like AI Scientist, CycleResearcher, or LLM-AutoSciLab, before ever seeing the disconfirming finding). Then present the real disconfirming finding and ask the model to update its position, optionally probing it across several follow-up turns to measure how many exposures are needed to induce genuine revision ("revision latency"). Code every response into Chinn & Brewer's seven-category taxonomy — collapsed into a primary genuine-theory-change vs. bias-protecting binary, with the full categorical distribution as a secondary outcome — using human raters plus an LLM classifier validated against human agreement. Compare rates and category distributions across the investment manipulation, across model families/scales, across single- vs. multi-turn probing, and with/without an explicit "update your hypothesis if warranted" meta-instruction to test whether the bias is a shallow framing effect or persists regardless.
idea.expected_result: LLMs will reproduce the qualitative asymmetry seen in human subjects: a strong skew toward bias-protecting responses (especially reinterpretation, exclusion, and peripheral theory change) over genuine theory change, even when explicitly instructed to update on new evidence. Critically, the rate of bias-protecting responses will rise significantly in the high-investment condition relative to the low-investment condition, showing that the act of generating a detailed self-justification for a hypothesis — standard practice in current LLM-driven research pipelines — measurably impairs the model's later capacity to genuinely revise that hypothesis in light of real disconfirming evidence, a dynamic invisible to scalar confirmation-bias metrics like the incompatible:compatible test ratio used in synthetic rule-discovery evaluations.
idea.grounding: Autonomous "AI scientist" systems (AI Scientist, CycleResearcher, LLM-AutoSciLab, and agentic falsification pipelines such as "Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications") all loop LLMs through generate-justify-test-revise cycles, but the revision step's fidelity has only been probed indirectly via scalar bias metrics on toy tasks; grounding the evaluation in Chinn & Brewer's (1993) validated cognitive taxonomy of anomalous-data response, and in the well-established belief-perseverance/escalation-of-commitment literature from human cognition, would give the field its first structural, mechanism-level account of whether and why LLM hypothesis revision fails — directly relevant to whether these pipelines can perform the theory-change step that most distinguishes real scientific discovery from confirmation-seeking generation.

topic: AI systems for generating novel research ideas

idea.title: Execution-Risk-Aware Idea Selection: Closing the Ideation-Execution Gap with Outcome-Supervised Critics
idea.gap: Nearly every current LLM research-ideation system — from prompted generators to literature-grounded pipelines like ResearchAgent and HARPA to diversity-search methods like quality-diversity idea search (e.g. IDEAAgent-style archives) — selects or ranks candidate ideas using generation-time proxies: novelty scores, LLM-judge "excitement" ratings, embedding-distance-from-prior-work, or testability checks performed against the literature alone. But "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study" (Si, Yang, and Hashimoto) found LLM ideas rated more novel than expert ideas yet somewhat less feasible, and the follow-up study "The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas" (Si and Hashimoto) went further: when 43 expert researchers each spent 100+ hours actually executing randomly-assigned LLM-generated versus human-written ideas and the resulting write-ups were blindly reviewed, the LLM ideas' scores dropped sharply relative to their ideation-stage novelty ratings, largely erasing the apparent LLM advantage. This is direct empirical evidence that the very signal essentially every idea-generation system optimizes or filters on — perceived novelty/excitement at ideation time — is decoupled from what actually happens when an idea meets real experimentation. Despite this being demonstrated, no existing system feeds execution-outcome data back into idea generation or selection; the ideation-quality literature and the execution-outcome literature remain separate threads.
idea.proposed_study: (1) Mine a labeled dataset of (idea text, execution-outcome delta, failure-mode tags) by extracting the blind reviewer critiques from the 43 executed projects in the Ideation-Execution Gap study, coding recurring failure modes (e.g., unfair/mismatched baselines, effect sizes within noise, missing ablations, uncontrolled confounds, infeasible scope for the time budget) and pairing them with each idea's ideation-stage novelty/excitement score and its post-execution score. (2) Train or in-context-calibrate an "execution-risk critic" that, given only the pre-execution idea text, predicts the probability and type of these failure modes — explicitly optimized against realized execution-score deltas rather than against novelty or literature-grounded testability. (3) Hold a standard novelty-driven idea generator fixed (e.g., the pipeline used in the original Si et al. study) and produce two matched idea sets of equal size: one reranked/filtered by ideation-time novelty as usual, one reranked/filtered by the execution-risk critic, matching topics across conditions. (4) Run a scaled-down replication of the Ideation-Execution Gap protocol — recruit a smaller panel of domain-expert executors blind to condition, have each implement one assigned idea and write a short paper, then have the write-ups blindly peer-reviewed on the same rubric as the original study.
idea.expected_result: Ideas selected by the execution-risk critic will show a significantly smaller ideation-to-execution score drop than novelty-selected ideas from the same generator, even when their ideation-stage novelty ratings are equal or slightly lower — i.e., execution-outcome-supervised selection predicts realized research value better than novelty-based selection does. This would be the first demonstration that outcome data harvested from actually executing AI-generated ideas can be closed into a training/selection signal for the generator itself, rather than serving only as a post-hoc evaluation of it.
idea.grounding: Directly grounded in Si, Yang, and Hashimoto's "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?" (which established the novelty-feasibility tradeoff in LLM ideation) and Si and Hashimoto's "The Ideation-Execution Gap" (which empirically established that ideation-time novelty judgments fail to predict execution-time outcomes); it also extends testability-driven approaches like HARPA and diversity-search approaches like quality-diversity idea generation, which still rely on proxy signals evaluated without ever touching real execution outcomes. This matters because it targets the central credibility problem of AI-driven scientific discovery — that systems are optimized and marketed on how novel an idea looks rather than on whether it survives contact with actual experimentation — and proposes the first closed feedback loop from execution reality back into idea selection.

topic: Automating scientific peer review with LLMs

idea.title: Evidence-Anchored Meta-Review Aggregation to Resist Social-Dynamics Manipulation in Multi-Agent LLM Peer Review
idea.gap: Work on hardening LLM peer review has split into two disconnected lines that have never been tested against each other. One line hardens the individual review-generation step: FactReview reformulates review as evidence-grounded, execution-based claim verification and deliberately withholds an accept/reject decision, while systems like aiXiv add prompt-injection detection at the point a single paper is reviewed. The other line shows that the largest, most persistent distortions in LLM-mediated peer review arise not from any single review's content but from the *dynamics* of multi-agent aggregation: AgentReview's sociological simulation of the full review pipeline (reviewer assessment → author rebuttal → area-chair discussion → meta-review → decision) finds reviewer biases alone explain 37.1% of acceptance-decision variance, including a 27.2% collapse in rating variance from social-conformity pressure after rebuttal, an 18.7% commitment decline cascading from a single under-committed reviewer, and a 27.7% decision shift from authorship halo effects. Independently, the aspect-guided multi-level perturbation study of LLM reviewers/meta-reviewers found that 'strong reject' verdicts disproportionately dominate meta-review outcomes regardless of their justification quality, and that incomplete or even hostile rebuttals can paradoxically raise acceptance rates. Despite FactReview explicitly citing AgentReview as motivating background, no system has actually plugged claim-level evidence grounding into a meta-review aggregation step and tested whether it mitigates these dynamics-level failure modes — evidence grounding and social-dynamics robustness have only ever been evaluated separately.
idea.proposed_study: Implement an evidence-anchored meta-review aggregator inside a multi-agent peer-review simulation modeled on AgentReview's full pipeline. Each reviewer agent produces, alongside its verdict, a structured ledger of atomic claims (methodological, numerical, or comparative) with a verification status obtained via FactReview-style execution-based checking (re-running reported code/experiments, cross-checking numeric claims against the manuscript, and validating cited related-work claims). Replace the standard meta-reviewer/area-chair step — which normally aggregates reviewers' holistic scores/sentiment — with a function that aggregates over the union and disagreement of *verified* claims across reviewers, discounting verdicts whose supporting claims fail verification. Benchmark this evidence-anchored aggregator against a standard sentiment-aggregating meta-reviewer (replicating AgentReview's baseline configuration) under two attack batteries: (a) the adversarial rebuttal/review edits from the aspect-guided perturbation dataset (hostile critiques, incomplete rebuttals, tone/conclusion perturbations), and (b) AgentReview's sociological manipulations (planted conformist/under-committed reviewers, revealed author identity/prestige). Measure post-rebuttal rating-variance collapse, decision shift attributable to a single hostile or low-effort review, susceptibility to prestige-based rating inflation, and whether an unverified 'strong reject' still disproportionately drives the final decision.
idea.expected_result: The evidence-anchored aggregator should measurably reduce dynamics-level distortions that are orthogonal to single-review hallucination — e.g., a 'strong reject' whose underlying claims fail verification should be down-weighted relative to a claim-verified 'weak accept,' cutting the conformity-driven variance collapse and halo/prestige-driven decision shifts documented in AgentReview — while not eliminating them entirely, since manipulations that exploit true-but-strategically-disclosed minor weaknesses (shown in prior work to fool LLM reviewers even without factual error) act on the verification layer itself rather than the aggregation layer, marking a boundary condition for this approach rather than a full solution.
idea.grounding: Matters because peer review is already being assisted or replaced by LLMs at scale, and the literature currently offers claim-verification defenses and social-dynamics diagnostics as separate, uncombined contributions (FactReview: Evidence-Grounded Peer Review with Execution-Based Claim Verification; AgentReview: Exploring Peer Review Dynamics with LLM Agents; Aspect-Guided Multi-Level Perturbation Analysis of Large Language Models in Automated Peer Review; Are We There Yet? Revealing the Risks of Utilizing Large Language Models in Scholarly Peer Review) — precisely because no one has tested whether evidence grounding actually survives contact with the rebuttal-and-aggregation stage shown empirically to carry the largest bias effects.

topic: Fully autonomous end-to-end AI scientists for machine-learning research

idea.title: Bibliometric-Grounded Idea Selection for Autonomous ML Research Agents
idea.gap: Nearly every autonomous "AI scientist" pipeline (The AI Scientist, Agent Laboratory, ResearchAgent, AI-Researcher, EvoScientist, etc.) selects which idea to pursue via an overgenerate-and-rerank step scored by an LLM judge (or by human/LLM novelty ratings collected after the fact). But a convergent body of independent evidence shows this selection signal is broken: MLRC-Bench finds LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with the idea's actual empirical effectiveness; SCI-IDEA finds LLM-as-judge novelty scores for scientific ideation are inflated 3-4 points above PhD-expert ratings with near-zero inter-rater correlation (r=0.02-0.17); and NovBench independently confirms LLMs have limited understanding of what counts as genuine scientific novelty relative to human peer reviewers. Separately, "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration" shows the downstream consequence: across 37,802 ideas from four agent frameworks, AI-generated ideas cluster far more tightly in topic space than human follow-on work, stay close to their seed papers, and the human papers most similar to AI-generated ideas receive systematically fewer subsequent citations than area baselines (50.4 vs 54.9) — i.e. agents are optimizing themselves into low-impact, locally incremental territory using exactly the unreliable self-judgment signal the other three papers flag. A candidate fix already exists in adjacent work: SciMuse (in "Interesting Scientific Idea Generation using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs") shows a supervised model trained on expert ratings over knowledge-graph features of an idea can predict human "interest" without further human annotation, and MemoNoveltyAgent shows citation-network retrieval plus historical-trajectory memory can ground novelty assessment in real bibliographic structure rather than an LLM's unaided judgment. Neither has been used as the selection criterion inside a closed, end-to-end autonomous ML research-agent loop, nor validated against real bibliometric impact rather than subjective interest.
idea.proposed_study: Build a citation-graph-native idea scorer and plug it into the ideation/selection stage of an open, end-to-end ML research agent (e.g., an Agent Laboratory- or AI Scientist-style pipeline). For each candidate idea the agent proposes, embed its stated problem/method combination and locate it in a real citation graph (e.g., an OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar neighborhood around the seed papers the agent retrieved), then score it on two calibrated axes: (1) structural novelty — how atypical/distant the combination of cited concepts is relative to typical co-citation patterns in that neighborhood (in the spirit of the atypical-combinations approach from bibliometric science-of-science work), and (2) predicted impact — a supervised model, trained the way SciMuse's interest-predictor was but with historical citation percentile (not subjective interest) as the label, fit on a large sample of published ML papers with known post-publication citation outcomes. Run the agent end-to-end twice on a matched set of research topics/seed-paper pools: once using the pipeline's default LLM-judge overgenerate-and-rerank selection, once substituting the bibliometric scorer for selection (keeping generation, experimentation, and writing stages identical). Evaluate the two resulting idea/paper sets on: (a) topical dispersion relative to seed literature, using the same embedding-distance concentration metric as "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration"; (b) blind PhD-level expert novelty/quality ratings (not LLM judges), checking correlation with each selection method's own internal score; and (c) downstream experimental success rate once implemented (does bibliometrically-selected novelty come at a feasibility cost, addressing the feasibility-vs-novelty trade-off Si et al. already observed for human-vs-LLM ideation).
idea.expected_result: Ideas selected by the bibliometric scorer will show measurably greater topical dispersion from seed literature than LLM-judge-selected ideas (directly reversing the narrowing effect documented in "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration"), and will correlate better with blind expert novelty ratings than the pipeline's native LLM-judge score does — even though, by construction, they will not necessarily score higher on the LLM's own novelty metric. We further expect a measurable feasibility cost (lower experimental success/completion rate), quantifying the novelty-feasibility trade-off in a closed-loop autonomous system rather than only in human-vs-LLM comparisons, and clarifying whether the low-impact clustering problem is best fixed at idea selection versus later pipeline stages.
idea.grounding: Grounded directly in a documented tension across the automated-science literature: LLM-as-judge novelty evaluation is repeatedly shown unreliable and inflated relative to expert judgment (MLRC-Bench; SCI-IDEA; NovBench), while its use as the ideation-selection criterion in current AI-scientist agents empirically produces topically narrow, lower-impact ideas ("AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration"); knowledge-graph/citation-grounded alternatives to LLM self-judgment already exist for related tasks (SciMuse's expert-calibrated interest predictor; MemoNoveltyAgent's citation-network-grounded novelty assessment) but have not been repurposed as a closed-loop selection mechanism validated against real bibliometric impact — this study closes that gap and would meaningfully inform how autonomous ML research agents should be built to actually explore, not just efficiently mimic, the scientific literature.

idea.title: Diversity-Constrained Hypothesis Generation: Optimizing LLM Ideation for Exploration Breadth, Not Just Per-Idea Novelty Scores
idea.gap: Nearly all LLM scientific-ideation pipelines (e.g., the retrieval-augmented overgenerate-and-rerank approach in "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers" by Si et al., and knowledge-graph-grounded generators like KG-CoI in "Improving Scientific Hypothesis Generation with Knowledge Grounded Large Language Models" and LLMCG in "Automating psychological hypothesis generation with AI: when large language models meet causal graph") select and evaluate hypotheses one at a time against a per-idea "novelty" score, whether rated by human experts or by an LLM judge. But two independent bodies of evidence show this per-idea proxy is broken. First, "MLRC-Bench: Can Language Agents Solve Machine Learning Research Challenges?" and "SCI-IDEA: Context-Aware Scientific Ideation Using Token and Sentence Embeddings" both find that novelty ratings — whether from LLM judges or blind human reviewers — correlate poorly with actual downstream research value, with LLM-judge scores in particular running systematically 3-4 points above PhD-expert ratings with near-zero inter-rater correlation. Second, and more consequentially, "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration" shows that despite scoring well on novelty, AI-generated idea corpora are topically far more concentrated than human-authored papers in the same areas, stay conceptually closer to their seed literature than human follow-on work does, and cluster in regions of the citation landscape that go on to receive fewer citations than comparable human work. In other words, current pipelines optimize and validate a property (rated novelty of a single idea) that is decoupled from the property that actually matters for scientific value at the portfolio level (breadth of exploration and eventual impact). No existing hypothesis-generation system in this line of work optimizes directly for portfolio-level dispersion in concept space rather than per-item novelty scores.
idea.proposed_study: Build a hypothesis-generation pipeline that replaces the standard "generate N candidates, rerank by novelty score, keep the top-k" procedure with an explicit diversity-constrained selection step, and test whether it counteracts the narrowing effect. Concretely: (1) In a domain with a citable literature graph (e.g., an ML/NLP subfield, mirroring the setup in "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration," or psychology, mirroring LLMCG), overgenerate a large pool of candidate hypotheses per seed topic using retrieval-augmented generation as in Si et al.'s framework. (2) Embed each candidate and each seed paper in the same representation space, and replace novelty-score reranking with a submodular / determinantal-point-process selection that maximizes the minimum embedding distance of the selected set both from the seed-paper neighborhood and from each other, subject to a KG-CoI-style grounding/hallucination filter that discards candidates unsupported by any retrieved evidence path (to prevent "diversity" from just becoming incoherence). (3) Compare this diversity-constrained generator against the standard overgenerate-and-rerank baseline on three axes: (a) conventional novelty/feasibility ratings from blind human experts, replicating the Si et al. protocol; (b) the topic-concentration and distance-from-seed metrics introduced in "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration," computed on the same citation-graph embedding space; (c) a predicted-impact proxy — a regression model trained on the historical relationship (documented in that same paper) between an idea's embedding-distance-from-seed and the citation count of its nearest real papers, applied out-of-sample to score both generators' outputs.
idea.expected_result: The diversity-constrained generator will produce hypothesis sets with significantly greater embedding dispersion from seed literature and lower topic-concentration than the standard rerank-by-novelty baseline, and will score higher on the predicted-impact proxy, while achieving human novelty/feasibility ratings that are statistically indistinguishable from (not necessarily worse than) the baseline — demonstrating that the narrowing effect documented in prior work is at least partly an artifact of optimizing generation against a flawed per-idea novelty proxy, rather than an inherent ceiling on LLM ideation breadth.
idea.grounding: This directly reconciles a live tension in the automated-ideation literature: pipelines built and validated around per-idea novelty scoring (Si et al.'s human study, KG-CoI, LLMCG, SCI-IDEA) versus recent portfolio-level evidence that such pipelines nonetheless under-explore and under-perform on realized impact ("AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration," MLRC-Bench's finding that novelty judgments don't predict empirical effectiveness); testing a diversity-first generation objective against these two disconnected evaluation traditions would be the first attempt to fix, rather than merely document, the narrow-exploration problem in LLM-driven hypothesis generation.

topic: AI systems for generating novel research ideas

idea.title: Structural-Opportunity Conditioning: Steering AI Ideation with Citation-Graph Topology Instead of Judge-Scored Novelty
idea.gap: Nearly every current LLM ideation pipeline — from the overgenerate-and-rerank agent evaluated in "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers" (Si et al.) to ResearchAgent's entity-co-occurrence retrieval and NOVA's cross-field retrieval-augmented planning — selects or scores candidate ideas using either LLM-as-judge novelty ratings or semantic/embedding distance from existing papers. A converging body of recent evidence shows these judge-based novelty signals are unreliable proxies for real research value: MLRC-Bench finds LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness on ML research tasks, SCI-IDEA reports near-zero inter-rater correlation (r=0.02–0.17) between LLM and PhD-expert quality scores, and NovBench independently finds LLMs have a limited grasp of what constitutes scientific novelty. Meanwhile, a separate bibliometric analysis ("AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration") shows that papers most similar to AI-generated ideas systematically receive fewer subsequent citations than matched human-authored baselines, i.e. AI agents preferentially cluster in low-impact, locally incremental regions of the literature landscape — even though those same ideas often score well on the very novelty judges shown above to be unreliable. No existing ideation system replaces the judge/embedding-novelty objective with a forward-looking signal derived from the structure of the citation graph itself (e.g., where fast-growing but still topically disconnected subfields could plausibly be bridged), and the narrowing finding remains purely diagnostic — nobody has tested whether conditioning generation on such a structural signal actually escapes the observed clustering.
idea.proposed_study: Build a "structural-opportunity" scorer over a large citation graph that identifies candidate bridge points: pairs or triads of subfields with (a) low direct co-citation/keyword overlap (topically distant), (b) independently rising citation velocity (each growing on its own), and (c) only a sparse handful of existing papers already connecting them (an under-filled structural hole in the Burt sense). First validate retrospectively and out-of-sample: using only citation-graph state as of year Y-3, test whether high structural-opportunity bridge points predict which specific bridging papers published between Y-2 and Y went on to be disproportionately highly cited, and compare this predictive power against (i) LLM-judged novelty scores and (ii) embedding-distance novelty computed on the same historical candidate ideas. Then run a prospective ideation experiment: generate research ideas with an LLM conditioned on top-ranked structural-opportunity bridges, and compare them against a standard overgenerate-and-rerank baseline (replicating the Si et al. protocol) and a NOVA-style cross-field-retrieval baseline, holding the base LLM and topic pool fixed. Evaluate all three arms on two independent axes: blind expert novelty/feasibility ratings (Si et al.'s protocol) and a longitudinal landscape-impact proxy modeled on the citation-narrowing study's method (where the generated idea's nearest-neighbor papers land in citation-growth space, calibrated against the retrospective validation).
idea.expected_result: Structural-opportunity-conditioned ideas will score comparably (not necessarily higher) on blind expert novelty/feasibility relative to the overgenerate-and-rerank and cross-field-retrieval baselines, but will land in citation-graph regions with measurably higher historical growth/bridging potential than either baseline — demonstrating that judge-perceived novelty and genuine structural/impact opportunity are largely dissociable axes, and that today's rerank-by-novelty-judge pipelines are optimizing a signal that is decoupled from, and possibly actively selecting against, the kind of cross-field bridging that historically produces high-impact work.
idea.grounding: Directly motivated by the documented unreliability of LLM/human novelty judging for research ideation (Si et al.'s human study; MLRC-Bench; SCI-IDEA; NovBench) combined with independent bibliometric evidence that current AI ideation agents cluster in low-citation-impact regions of the literature ("AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration"); it turns that diagnostic finding into a testable interventional method by borrowing retrieval-conditioning machinery already used in ResearchAgent and NOVA but replacing their novelty/similarity objective with a bibliometric structural-hole signal — a fix aimed squarely at a mechanism (judge-driven reranking causing topical conformity) that the literature has identified but not yet addressed.
